newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE coffee futures pare losses, origin sales ebb.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE coffee futures pare losses, origin sales ebb.

text.p: London robusta coffee futures ignored pre-market calls of $100-$200 down to open about $60-70 lower, and moved futher to cut some losses by Friday midsession in good two-way trade activity.
Traders said the market was probably heading for a pause, consolidating its recent gains after a new rally to $1,825 a tonne basis May, a peak not seen since last June.
Friday's slide was also halted by a dearth of sellers notably from Asia on the sharply lower call.
"We have done better than it was technically due this morning and that's purely because you're not seeing the same origin selling coming out from the Far East," said one.
By the midday close, benchmark May stood just $56 lower at $1,638 a tonne after hitting the session's floor of $1,615 and a high of $1,648.
Coffee was called to open a sharp $200 down in theory after heavy New York losses overnight but traders said London could be content with $100 lower.
Technically, May faces strong support at the $1,600 level while the upside goal is pegged at a chart gap of between $1,702 and $1,728, Thursday's high and Wedneday's low respectively.
New York's arabica futures, retracing further from a new rally earlier in the week, came under severe pressure on Thursday.
Persistent speculative profit-taking pulled the benchmark May to a low of 181 cents a lb before finishing seven percent down at 182.25.
Traders said perception of a slight easing of supply concerns also contributed to the sell-off.
London traders called the New York market five cents up on paper on Friday but added they were not suprised if it came in close to unchanged.
Midday volume reached a scant 2,203 lots. March/May switch was traded at a premium of $3 and July/Sept at $9 but turnover was meagre.
Earlier on Friday, traders in Vietnam said the country's coffee trade came to a virtual halt on Friday amid sharp falls in international prices.

Traders estimated that some 50,000-60,000 tonnes of coffee from Vietnam's 1996/97 harvest remained unsold, after around 200,000 tonnes having been marketed. -- Jalil Hamid, London newsroom +44 171 542 4985 gapped higher-than-excpectbucked pre-opening expectations of $100-$200 lower and moved to cut further losses were barely moved in the afternoon and prices ended Thursday lower on early selling activity.

Conditions were dull and interest was dominated by nearby May/July switches. Market players said trade interest had been negligible with the bulk of trading was in the hands of locals and commission houses.
The benchmark May contract hit a high of $1,702 but closed just below the $1,700 mark, finishing $41 down at at $1,694 a tonne. It saw the day's low of $1,672.
Overall volume reached 5,328 lots.
New York arabica futures showed losses by midday U.S. trading but benchmark May found some support at 191.00 cents level.
With the fading upward momentum in New York, traders said the London market looked vulnerable to further decline, adding that May robustas could find some strong support at $1,660.
A test below $1,660 would signal that the recent rally had finished for the time being.
Both markets are looking forward to next week's producer talks in London, expected to consider the current high prices and their impact on consumption.
Brazil's government said it would not decide on any position ahead of the May 20 meeting of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries's technical group.

But Indonesia said the grouping should consider the interests of consumers while Ivory Coast maintained that extra export cuts of 1.3 million 60-kg bags in the first half of 1997 -- agreed in January -- should be fully implemented, saying the ACPC's credibility was at stake. -- Jalil Hamid, London newsroom +44 171 542 4985
